title: Note Making and Summarisation
tagline: A 200–250 word passage converted into numbered notes with a key, then into a summary of fifty words: format, content and expression.

overview.intro: The second task of Section A asks you to read a passage of about 200–250 words and produce two things from it: a set of notes worth 5 marks and a summary of up to 50 words worth 3 marks. The marks are split between content and format in a way that rewards method — a title, correct numbering and indenting, a glossary and notes that capture the passage’s structure rather than its sentences. This unit teaches the format precisely, then the discipline of writing a summary that fits the word limit without losing the argument.

facts.label: Notes
facts.value: 5 marks — title 1, numbering and indenting 1, key/glossary 1, notes 2.

facts.label: Summary
facts.value: 3 marks — content 2, expression 1; up to 50 words.

learningOutcomes: Identify the main idea and the hierarchy of supporting points in a passage.
Produce notes in the prescribed format with title, numbering, indenting and a key.
Write a summary within fifty words that keeps the passage’s argument.
Allocate time between the notes and the summary.

blocks.text: Notes are a compression of structure, not a set of sentences. Read the passage once to find its governing idea — the point every paragraph serves — and then treat each paragraph as either a main point under that idea or a subdivision of a point already found. Main points become the numbered top level; the details beneath them become lettered sub-points; examples and illustrations are dropped unless they carry the point themselves. The test for anything you include is simple: if removing it would leave the reader with the same understanding of the passage’s argument, it does not belong in the notes.

rows: The central idea the passage develops
The writer’s name, date or incidental framing
Restatements of a point in other words
Sub-points that qualify or divide a main point
Single examples that illustrate but do not extend
Contrasts where they carry the argument

items: Notes must be telegraphic: the verb and its object, nothing else.
Every main point gets its own number; never merge two into one line.
Indent sub-points clearly so the hierarchy is visible at a glance.
Read the finished notes alone: they should rebuild the argument without the passage.

blocks.text: One of the five marks is explicitly for numbering and indenting, which means the layout is examined, not merely helpful. Number the main points 1, 2, 3 in Roman or Arabic numerals consistently; indent sub-points beneath their parent and mark them a, b, c; and keep every line flush with its own level. The title carries another mark: it must be a noun phrase covering the whole passage — three or four words that would work as a heading in a contents page, not a sentence and not a fragment copied from the first line.

The key or glossary carries the third mark. List the words a general reader might not know — technical terms, unusual nouns, the writer’s coinages — in alphabetical order, and give a short gloss for each. Terms already in ordinary use do not belong here; a glossary of easy words looks like padding. The remaining two marks are for the notes themselves, which is where content accuracy is judged: points must be drawn from the passage, correctly hierarchised, and free of distortion.

blocks.caption: How the 5 marks are earned
rows: A noun phrase covering the entire passage
Difficult terms in order with short glosses
Accurate main points and sub-points in hierarchy

learn.title: Writing the summary in fifty words

blocks.text: The summary carries 3 marks: 2 for content and 1 for expression, in up to 50 words. Content means the passage’s central idea and its principal supporting points in proportion — a summary that captures one detail out of four has failed regardless of its English. Expression means a single connected piece of prose in reported form, without bullet points, without the writer’s name and without examples that the passage used only to illustrate. Fifty words is roughly two sentences of average length or three short ones, which is enough for the idea plus two supporting points, not for everything.

The working method is to draft from the notes you have just made rather than from the passage again: the notes already contain the hierarchy, so the summary becomes a compression of the notes, which is itself a compression of the passage. Count the words before writing the final version, and cut first from examples and qualifiers rather than from the main points, since the content marks depend on coverage and the expression marks on fluency. Beginning with “The passage…” or “According to the writer…” costs two or three of your fifty words and buys nothing.

items.text: Passage: four paragraphs on urban trees, with one species named as an example.
items.note: A summary naming the species but omitting the argument about canopy cover has inverted the content marks.

items.text: A 52-word draft with the final clause removed.
items.note: Trimming the closing hedge rather than a main point keeps content and fits the limit.

blocks.text: This task sits between the passages and the grammar section, and it rewards students who keep it tight: the passage is short, the format is fixed, and the eight marks available are quickly won once the structure is habitual. The commonest losses are structural rather than intellectual — no title, numbering that restarts or levels out, a glossary of trivial words, notes written in full sentences, and a summary that exceeds fifty words because it was drafted without counting.

Practice should therefore be done to a clock with the format checked afterwards against the mark scheme rather than against your own impression. Two habits raise the score reliably: reading the notes back as a stand-alone document to see whether the argument survives, and counting the summary before submission rather than after. Both take seconds and address the exact elements the marks are attached to.

questions.prompt: State how the five marks for notes are distributed.
questions.answer: The five marks are distributed as: 1 for the title, which must be a noun phrase covering the whole passage; 1 for numbering and indenting, which requires consistent levels with sub-points visibly indented beneath their parents; 1 for the key or glossary of difficult terms in order with short meanings; and 2 for the notes themselves, judged on accurate main points and sub-points arranged in hierarchy and drawn only from the passage.
questions.explanation: All four elements must be named with their marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a main point and a sub-point, and give the test for what to exclude.
questions.answer: A main point states one of the distinct ideas the passage develops in support of its governing idea, and each gets its own number at the first level. A sub-point divides, qualifies or exemplifies a main point beneath which it sits, and is indented and lettered so the hierarchy is visible. The test for exclusion is functional: if removing a line would leave the reader with the same understanding of the passage’s argument, it does not belong. On that test, repetition in different words, the writer’s incidental framing, connectives and sentence furniture are all excluded, and single examples are excluded unless they carry a point rather than merely illustrate it. A further practical test is to read the notes alone: anything the reader needs but cannot find indicates a point wrongly dropped, and anything that adds nothing indicates one wrongly kept.
questions.explanation: Both the distinction and the exclusion test must be stated with the practical check that follows from them.

questions.prompt: Describe the process of writing a summary that fits fifty words without losing the passage’s argument.
questions.answer: The process begins with the notes rather than with the passage, because the notes have already compressed the passage’s hierarchy. First identify what the passage is centrally arguing or describing, so that the summary’s opening clause states the governing idea rather than a detail. Next select the two principal supporting points — the ones without which the argument would not stand — and reject the rest, including examples, since fifty words will not hold them. Draft these into connected prose in reported form, using one sentence for the central idea and one or two for the support, avoiding the empty openings that cost words without adding content. Then count the words before finalising: at an average of twelve to fifteen words a sentence, three sentences is the realistic maximum, and a fourth almost always breaches the limit. If the draft is long, cut in a fixed order — qualifiers first, then examples, then any point that repeats another — because content marks depend on covering the governing idea and the principal support while expression marks depend on fluency, and cutting main points damages the larger share of the total. Finally, reread for expression: reported form, one connected piece, no bullet points, no author’s name, and no comment on the passage. The discipline that produces the marks is therefore compression of the right material in the right order, verified by a word count.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the sequence from notes to selection to drafting to counting, and an explicit order for cutting when the limit is exceeded.

questions.prompt: In this task the marks are lost to format more often than to meaning. Discuss.
questions.answer: The mark scheme itself supports the claim, because format is separately and generously weighted. Of the five marks for notes, two are awarded purely for layout — the title and the numbering with indenting — and another for the glossary’s organisation, which means a student who has understood the passage completely can still drop three of five marks by omitting a title, letting levels run together, or filling the key with easy words. The summary adds a further structural hazard: the fifty-word limit is a hard boundary, and exceeding it costs content or expression marks regardless of the quality of the understanding behind it. Teachers see this pattern repeatedly — notes written in full sentences, numbering that restarts, sub-points indented no differently from main points, summaries of seventy words written with no count. The counter-argument is that format errors are rarely innocent. A student who cannot find the governing idea will produce no title worth marking; a student who has not seen the hierarchy will indent nothing; and a summary that overruns usually overruns because the writer never decided which points mattered, which is a failure of content selection rather than of handwriting. On this reading format is where content failure becomes visible rather than where it is replaced. The judgement that best fits the evidence is therefore that the two are coupled but not equal: format is the more frequent site of lost marks because it is explicit, checkable in seconds and habit-dependent, while meaning is the deeper dependency that determines whether there is any structure to format. Practically, the claim is sound advice — verify title, indenting, glossary and word count every time — provided the verification follows a first read that has genuinely found the argument.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the mark-scheme evidence, the counter-argument that format reflects content, and a judgement separating frequency of error from depth of cause.
